lessons.title: Synthetic and natural polymers
lessons.summary: Discover how small molecules link into enormous chains to make plastics, fibres and the molecules of life, and learn the difference between addition and condensation polymerisation.
objectives: I can describe addition polymerisation and draw the repeating unit of an addition polymer from its monomer.
I can describe condensation polymerisation and explain how it differs from addition polymerisation.
I can identify the monomers and linkages in polyesters and polyamides.
I can describe the natural polymers DNA, proteins, starch and cellulose and name their monomers.

activities.title: What is a polymer?
activities.content:
## Long chains from small pieces

A **polymer** is a very large molecule made by joining together thousands of small molecules called **monomers**. The word comes from Greek: *poly* means many, *mer* means part.

Think of a paper chain. Each paper strip is a monomer. Link hundreds together and you have a polymer. The chain has the same basic pattern repeated over and over, which is why we describe a polymer by its **repeating unit**.

Polymers are everywhere:

- **Synthetic** polymers made in factories: poly(ethene) in carrier bags, poly(propene) in ropes and crates, PVC in window frames, nylon in clothing.
- **Natural** polymers made by living things: starch and cellulose in plants, proteins in muscle, DNA in every cell.

### Why polymers behave differently from their monomers

Ethene is a gas you cannot see. Poly(ethene) is a tough, flexible solid. The chains are so long that there are strong **intermolecular forces** between them, holding the solid together, even though each individual force is weak. Longer chains mean stronger forces and a stronger, higher-melting polymer.

There are two ways monomers can be joined: **addition** and **condensation** polymerisation.

activities.title: Addition polymerisation
activities.content:
## Opening double bonds

**Addition polymerisation** uses monomers that are **alkenes**, because they have a C=C double bond. Under high pressure and with a catalyst, the double bonds open up and the monomers join end to end. **Nothing else is produced**: the polymer is the only product.

ethene → poly(ethene)

### Drawing the repeating unit

**Monomer:**

```
  H   H
   \ /
    C=C
   / \
  H   H
```

**Repeating unit:**

```
    H   H
    |   |
  -(C - C)-
    |   |
    H   H     n
```

The rules:

1. Change the **double bond to a single bond**.
2. Draw a **bond sticking out on each side** to show the chain continues.
3. Put the unit in **brackets** with a small **n** to mean "repeated many times".
4. Keep every other atom exactly where it was.

The **n** appears on both sides of the equation: n C₂H₄ → –(C₂H₄)ₙ–

### Other addition polymers

| Monomer | Polymer | Use |
|---|---|---|
| propene | poly(propene) | crates, rope |
| chloroethene | poly(chloroethene), PVC | pipes, cables |
| tetrafluoroethene | PTFE | non-stick pans |

Whatever is attached to the double-bonded carbons simply stays attached in the polymer.

activities.title: Worked example: from monomer to repeating unit
activities.content:
**Draw the repeating unit of poly(propene) from propene, CH₂=CH–CH₃.**

**Step 1:** draw the monomer with the double bond horizontal and all four groups shown.

```
  H   CH₃
   \ /
    C=C
   / \
  H   H
```

**Step 2:** open the double bond into a single bond and extend a bond out on each side.

```
    H   CH₃
    |   |
  -(C - C)-
    |   |
    H   H     n
```

The CH₃ group is untouched. It hangs off the chain as a side group.

**Going backwards: a polymer has the repeating unit –(CHCl–CH₂)ₙ–. What is the monomer?**

Put the double bond back between the two carbons and remove the bonds out the sides: **CHCl=CH₂**, which is chloroethene. The polymer is poly(chloroethene), better known as PVC.

**Common error:** leaving the double bond in the repeating unit. Once the monomers have joined, that double bond has been used up.

question.text: Which of these molecules could be used as a monomer for addition polymerisation?
question.hint: Addition polymerisation needs a C=C double bond.
question.explanation: Only ethene, C₂H₄, is an alkene with a double bond. Ethane and propane are alkanes and ethanol is an alcohol; none of these has a C=C bond.

options.feedback: Ethane has only single bonds, so it cannot undergo addition.

question.text: Complete the sentences about addition polymerisation.

metadata.blanksText: Addition polymers are made from monomers that contain a carbon–carbon ___ bond. During the reaction this bond opens and the monomers join to form a long chain. The polymer is the ___ product. The small letter ___ in the formula shows that the unit is repeated many times.

question.hint: Alkenes have a special type of bond. Nothing else is made. Think of the symbol in –(C₂H₄)ₙ–.
question.explanation: The monomers contain a C=C double bond; the polymer is the only product; n shows the number of repeats.

activities.title: Condensation polymerisation
activities.content:
## Joining with a small molecule lost

**Condensation polymerisation** is different in three ways:

1. The monomers usually have **two functional groups**, one at each end (for example –OH at both ends, or –COOH at both ends).
2. Each time two monomers join, a **small molecule**, usually **water**, is released.
3. Often **two different monomers** are used, which join alternately.

### Polyesters

A polyester is made from a **diol** (two –OH groups) and a **dicarboxylic acid** (two –COOH groups). Each –OH reacts with a –COOH to form an **ester link** and release a water molecule.

n HO–[  ]–OH + n HOOC–[  ]–COOH → –[ O–[  ]–O–CO–[  ]–CO ]ₙ– + 2n H₂O

Because each monomer has a reactive group at **both** ends, the chain can keep growing in both directions.

Polyester fibres are used in clothing, and PET (a polyester) is the plastic in drinks bottles.

### Polyamides

A polyamide is made from a **diamine** (two –NH₂ groups) and a dicarboxylic acid. The link formed is an **amide link**. Nylon is a polyamide.

### Comparing the two types

| | Addition | Condensation |
|---|---|---|
| Monomer | alkene with C=C | two functional groups per molecule |
| Number of monomer types | one | usually two |
| Other product | none | small molecule (water) |
| Example | poly(ethene) | polyester, nylon |

activities.title: Worked example: counting water molecules
activities.content:
**Ethanediol, HO–CH₂–CH₂–OH, reacts with hexanedioic acid, HOOC–(CH₂)₄–COOH, to make a polyester. How many water molecules are made for every pair of monomers that react?**

Each –OH reacts with one –COOH. One diol molecule has two –OH groups and one diacid has two –COOH groups.

When one diol and one diacid have both been fully built into the chain, all **two** –OH groups and all **two** –COOH groups have reacted, forming **two ester links** and releasing **two water molecules**.

So for n of each monomer, **2n** water molecules are released, which matches the general equation.

**What would happen if a monomer only had ONE –OH group?**

It could join to the chain once, but there would be no reactive group left on its other end. The chain would **stop growing**. That is why condensation monomers must have two functional groups.

**Higher-tier tip:** in the exam you may be given a simplified box notation, HO–[box]–OH, and asked to draw the polymer. Keep the boxes, join O to C=O, and take out H₂O each time.

question.text: Which statements about condensation polymerisation are correct? Select all that apply.
question.explanation: Condensation polymerisation produces a small molecule such as water each time monomers join, and the monomers need two functional groups. It does not use C=C bonds and the polymer is not the only product.

options.text: A small molecule such as water is produced.
The monomers have two functional groups each.
The monomers must contain a C=C double bond.
The polymer is the only product.
options.feedback: Water (or another small molecule) is also formed.

question.text: In a condensation polymerisation, 500 molecules of a diol react with 500 molecules of a dicarboxylic acid to form one long chain. How many water molecules are released? (Ignore the end groups.)
question.hint: Each pair of monomers that fully joins into the chain forms two ester links.
question.explanation: 2n water molecules for n of each monomer: 2 × 500 = 1000.

activities.title: Natural polymers
activities.content:
## Polymers made by living things

Nature was making polymers long before chemists were. Here are the four you need.

### DNA

**DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid)** carries the genetic instructions of every living thing. It is made of two polymer strands twisted into a **double helix**. The monomers are called **nucleotides**. There are four different nucleotides, and the order they appear in along the chain is the genetic code.

### Proteins

**Proteins** are polymers of **amino acids**. Amino acids have an amine group (–NH₂) at one end and a carboxylic acid group (–COOH) at the other, so they join by **condensation polymerisation**, releasing water and forming amide (peptide) links. Glycine, H₂N–CH₂–COOH, is the simplest amino acid.

Different sequences of amino acids give different proteins: enzymes, muscle fibres, hair and the haemoglobin in your blood.

### Starch and cellulose

Both are polymers of **sugars** (glucose). Plants make starch to **store energy** and cellulose to build strong **cell walls**. The difference is in how the glucose units are joined, which makes starch digestible and cellulose not.

| Natural polymer | Monomer | Job |
|---|---|---|
| DNA | nucleotides | stores genetic information |
| protein | amino acids | enzymes, structure |
| starch | glucose (sugar) | energy store in plants |
| cellulose | glucose (sugar) | plant cell walls |

question.text: Match each natural polymer to its monomer.
question.hint: Two of them share the same monomer.
question.explanation: DNA is made of nucleotides, proteins of amino acids, and both starch and cellulose are made of glucose.

question.text: Put the steps in order to draw the repeating unit of an addition polymer from its alkene monomer.
question.hint: You must start with the monomer drawn correctly before changing anything.
question.explanation: Draw the monomer, open the double bond, add the bonds out each side, then add brackets and n.
order: Draw the monomer with all four groups on the double-bonded carbons
Replace the double bond with a single bond
Draw a bond extending out of the unit on each side
Add brackets and the letter n

question.text:
Poly(ethene) is made from ethene. Polyester is made from ethanediol and a dicarboxylic acid.

(a) Name the type of polymerisation used to make poly(ethene), and state what feature of ethene makes this possible.

(b) Name the type of polymerisation used to make polyester, and state what other product is formed.

(c) Explain why ethanediol has to have an –OH group at each end of the molecule.

(d) Explain why poly(ethene) is a solid at room temperature even though ethene is a gas.
question.hint: Think about double bonds, water, chain growth in two directions, and forces between long chains.
question.explanation: (a) Addition polymerisation; ethene has a C=C double bond. (b) Condensation polymerisation; water is also formed. (c) Each –OH can form one link, so two are needed for the molecule to join on both sides and allow the chain to keep growing. (d) The polymer chains are very long, so the intermolecular forces between them are much stronger than between small ethene molecules, and more energy is needed to separate them.

markScheme.criterion: Addition polymerisation because ethene has a C=C double bond
Two –OH groups are needed so the monomer can bond at both ends and the chain continues to grow
Long chains have stronger intermolecular forces, so more energy is needed to separate them

activities.title: Key points
activities.content:
- A **polymer** is a long chain made from many small **monomers**; it is described by its **repeating unit**.
- **Addition polymerisation**: alkene monomers, the C=C opens, monomers join, **no other product**. Repeating unit: single bond, bonds out each side, brackets and **n**.
- **Condensation polymerisation**: monomers with **two functional groups**, usually two different monomers, a **small molecule (water)** is released each time a link forms.
- **Polyesters**: diol + dicarboxylic acid, ester links. **Polyamides** (nylon): diamine + dicarboxylic acid.
- **Natural polymers**: DNA (nucleotides, double helix), proteins (amino acids), starch and cellulose (glucose).
- Long chains have strong **intermolecular forces**, which is why polymers are solids.

practiceQuestions.text: True or false: a monomer is a small molecule that can join with others to form a polymer.
practiceQuestions.explanation: True. Monomers are the building blocks; many monomers joined together form a polymer.

practiceQuestions.text: What is the monomer of poly(propene)?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Poly(propene) is made from propene, C₃H₆, by addition polymerisation.

options.feedback: Propane has no double bond and cannot polymerise.

metadata.blanksText: Proteins are natural polymers made from monomers called ___ ___, which join by condensation polymerisation.

practiceQuestions.hint: Two words; the first is a type of nitrogen-containing group, the second is what vinegar is.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Proteins are polymers of amino acids.

practiceQuestions.text: Which pair of monomers would form a polyester?
practiceQuestions.hint: An ester link forms between an –OH group and a –COOH group.
practiceQuestions.explanation: A diol (two –OH groups) and a dicarboxylic acid (two –COOH groups) form ester links and give a polyester.

options.text: a diol and a dicarboxylic acid

options.feedback: These are alkenes, used for addition polymers.

options.text: a diamine and a dicarboxylic acid
options.feedback: This combination makes a polyamide such as nylon.
Amino acids make proteins, which are polyamides.

practiceQuestions.text: A poly(ethene) chain contains 2000 repeating units. Calculate the relative formula mass of the chain. (Mr of the C₂H₄ repeating unit = 28; ignore the end groups.)
practiceQuestions.hint: Multiply the number of units by the mass of one unit.

practiceQuestions.text: Match each polymer to the type of polymerisation used to make it.
practiceQuestions.hint: Alkenes give addition polymers; anything with a link like ester or amide is condensation.
practiceQuestions.explanation: PVC is poly(chloroethene), an addition polymer. Nylon and proteins are polyamides made by condensation polymerisation; proteins are natural.

practiceQuestions.text: Which statements about DNA are correct? Select all that apply.
practiceQuestions.explanation: DNA is a double helix made from two polymer strands of nucleotide monomers. It is a natural polymer, not made from amino acids, and it is not an addition polymer of alkenes.

options.text: It is made of two strands twisted into a double helix.
It is made from amino acids.
It is an addition polymer made from alkenes.

practiceQuestions.text: The repeating unit of PVC is –(CH₂–CHCl)ₙ–. Calculate the relative formula mass of one repeating unit. (Ar: C = 12, H = 1, Cl = 35.5)
Describe how the repeating unit of poly(chloroethene) is drawn, starting from the monomer chloroethene, CH₂=CHCl.
practiceQuestions.hint: Three changes: the double bond, the side bonds, the brackets.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Change the C=C double bond to a single bond; draw a bond extending from each carbon out of the unit to show the chain continues; put the unit in brackets with n outside. The H atoms and Cl atom stay attached to the same carbons.

markScheme.criterion: The double bond is replaced by a single bond
Bonds are drawn extending out of each side of the unit
Brackets with n are used and the H and Cl atoms stay in place

practiceQuestions.text:
Glycine, H₂N–CH₂–COOH, is an amino acid. Many glycine molecules can join together to form a polymer.

(a) Name the type of polymer formed.

(b) Name the type of polymerisation, and explain how you can tell from the structure of glycine.

(c) Name the small molecule released when two glycine molecules join.

(d) Explain why proteins with different sequences of amino acids have different properties.
practiceQuestions.hint: Glycine has two functional groups. Think about what is lost when –NH₂ meets –COOH.
practiceQuestions.explanation: (a) A polypeptide / protein (a polyamide). (b) Condensation polymerisation, because glycine has two functional groups (–NH₂ and –COOH) rather than a C=C double bond. (c) Water. (d) The order of amino acids determines how the chain folds and what groups are exposed, so different sequences give different shapes and functions, such as different enzymes.

markScheme.criterion: Condensation polymerisation because glycine has two functional groups (–NH₂ and –COOH), not a C=C
Different sequence gives a different shape / structure, so a different function

practiceQuestions.text: A chemist wants to make an addition polymer. Which of these compounds could be used as the monomer?
practiceQuestions.hint: Addition polymerisation only works with molecules that contain a C=C double bond.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Propene, C₃H₆, is an alkene, so it has a C=C double bond that can open to join monomers together. Propane is a saturated alkane, propanol is an alcohol and ethanoic acid is a carboxylic acid; none of these has a C=C bond.

options.feedback: Propane has only single bonds, so there is no double bond to open.

practiceQuestions.text: Complete the sentences about how addition polymers are described.

metadata.blanksText: The small molecules that join together to form a polymer are called ___. In addition polymerisation these are ___, a family of hydrocarbons that contain a C=C double bond. The part of the polymer structure written inside the brackets is called the ___ unit.

practiceQuestions.hint: Poly- means many; the word for the small units starts with mono-. Ethene and propene belong to the family. The bracketed section is repeated over and over.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Monomers join to form polymers. In addition polymerisation the monomers are alkenes, which have a C=C double bond. The bracketed structure, drawn with n outside, is the repeating unit.

practiceQuestions.text: Which statements about addition polymerisation are correct? Select all that apply.
practiceQuestions.hint: Compare it with condensation polymerisation: what type of monomer is used and what is made?
practiceQuestions.explanation: In addition polymerisation the monomers are alkenes, whose C=C double bonds open so the molecules join, and the polymer is the only product. No small molecule such as water is lost, and the monomers do not need two functional groups.

options.text: The monomers contain a C=C double bond.
The polymer is the only product.
A small molecule such as water is lost each time two monomers join.
Each monomer must have two different functional groups.
options.feedback: Two functional groups are needed for condensation polymerisation, not addition.

practiceQuestions.text: Nylon is a condensation polymer. In one reaction, 320 molecules of a diamine react with 320 molecules of a dicarboxylic acid to form a single long chain, and one water molecule is released each time a link forms. How many water molecules are released? (Ignore the end groups.)
practiceQuestions.hint: Each diamine molecule forms a link at both of its ends.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Every monomer in the chain forms two links, one at each end, but each link is shared between two monomers. With 320 + 320 = 640 monomers there are 640 links, so 640 water molecules are released (equivalently 2 × 320).

practiceQuestions.text: Match each description to the natural polymer it describes.
practiceQuestions.hint: Two of the polymers are made from glucose but do different jobs in a plant.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Starch stores energy in plants and cellulose builds plant cell walls; both are made from glucose. DNA is a double strand of nucleotides carrying genetic information. Proteins, including enzymes, are made from amino acids.

pairs.left: stores energy in plants; made from glucose
builds plant cell walls; made from glucose
two strands of nucleotides that carry genetic information
made from amino acids; enzymes are examples

practiceQuestions.text: A student is given the repeating unit of an addition polymer and asked to draw the monomer. Put the steps in order.
practiceQuestions.hint: Start from the drawing you are given, remove what does not belong to a single molecule, and finish by restoring the alkene's key feature.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Copy the repeating unit without the brackets and n; remove the bonds that stick out on each side; change the single bond between the two backbone carbons back into a double bond; finally check every carbon has four bonds.
order: Copy the repeating unit without the brackets and the letter n
Remove the bonds that extend out of each side of the unit
Change the single bond between the two backbone carbons into a double bond
Check that every carbon atom has four bonds

practiceQuestions.text:
Poly(propene) is made from propene. Nylon is made from a diamine (a molecule with an –NH₂ group at each end) and a dicarboxylic acid.

(a) Name the type of polymerisation used to make poly(propene), and state the feature of propene that makes this possible.

(b) Name the type of polymerisation used to make nylon, and state the other product formed.

(c) Explain why the dicarboxylic acid must have a –COOH group at each end of the molecule.

(d) Propene is a gas at room temperature but poly(propene) is a solid. Explain why.
practiceQuestions.hint: Think about double bonds, a small molecule being lost, chain growth in both directions, and the forces between very long chains.
practiceQuestions.explanation: (a) Addition polymerisation; propene has a C=C double bond. (b) Condensation polymerisation; water is also formed. (c) Each –COOH group can form one link, so a group is needed at both ends for the molecule to bond on each side and allow the chain to keep growing. (d) Poly(propene) chains are very long, so the intermolecular forces between them are much stronger than between small propene molecules, and much more energy is needed to separate them.

markScheme.criterion: Addition polymerisation because propene has a C=C double bond
Two –COOH groups are needed so the monomer can bond at both ends and the chain continues to grow
Long chains have stronger intermolecular forces, so more energy is needed to separate them
